entry.title: Jaxnasium: Embracing PyTrees For Any-Agent, Cross-Suite Reinforcement Learning
entry.summary: Hardware-accelerated reinforcement learning in JAX has gained rapid popularity in recent years and has proven to be a successful method of scaling online reinforcement learning. The resulting ecosystem, however, is fragmented: environment suites define their own interfaces, and algorithm implementations are typically written for a single suite, a single type of space, and either JAX-native or host-based environments. Here we present Jaxnasium, a library for JAX-based reinforcement learning, aiming to make the field more accessible. Jaxnasium represents observation and action spaces as PyTrees, and uses this structure to build networks and support multi-agent processing. Through this, its near-single-file implementations run on discrete, continuous, image, and composite spaces, as well as in multi-agent environments, without any changes to the algorithm code. The same files serve as readable, research-friendly algorithms, as well as importable algorithms for more applied workloads. Through a minimal Gymnasium-style interface and wrappers for 11 suites, over 300 environments are available on which a small PPO implementation with default hyperparameters is able to run. Additionally, through a simple wrapper, we can run Gymnasium and EnvPool environments with the same algorithm and training loop, with no performance loss compared to architectures specifically built for training JAX algorithms on host-based environments. Jaxnasium further provides tools for multi-seed evaluation, hyperparameter sweeps, and project scaffolding. Jaxnasium is open-sourced at https://github.com/ponseko/jaxnasium

entry.title: Interpreting LLM Scores in Peer Review: Alignment and Divergence Across Prompts, Domains, and Manuscript Features
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) scores are being studied as information for scholarly evaluation. Interpreting these scores requires evidence about agreement with human judgments and its variation across evaluation conditions. Guided by an argument-based approach to validation, we compare four LLMs on 7,083 public ICLR 2024 submissions under a standard review condition and examine ten prompt conditions using DeepSeek-V3.2. We distinguish average score divergence, paper-level absolute error, and rank correlation, then examine domain differences and adjusted manuscript-feature associations. For DeepSeek-V3.2, Area Chair guidance reduces mean rating divergence from 1.460 to 0.199 points and mean absolute error from 1.577 to 0.942, while rank correlation changes from 0.377 to 0.387. Historical references combined with downward scoring instructions yield mean divergence of 0.052 and rank correlation of 0.321. Domain differences remain after global calibration. Longer titles have positive adjusted associations with rating divergence, and formula density has negative associations across all four configurations. These findings connect score interpretation to the scoring procedure, evaluation context, and manuscript information represented in the comparison. They show why aggregate alignment, manuscript ordering, and correspondence within manuscript groups require distinct evidence when evaluating LLM-generated scholarly assessment information.

entry.title: Is the arXiv Apocalypse upon us? A break in preprint growth coincident with agentic AI
entry.summary: As an experiment in agentic assisted analysis, we used an agentic AI model to analyse the effect of agentic AI on arXiv submissions; data acquisition, analysis and the first draft were carried out by the model under the author's direction. Monthly arXiv submissions have grown exponentially for three decades, at about $9\%$ per year. Fitting a piecewise log-linear trend with seasonal modulation to the full record, we find two post-pandemic breaks in growth rate. The first, in mid-2022, precedes ChatGPT and is carried by the expansion of AI research within computer science (CS); outside CS, growth from 2022 to 2025 remained at $8\%$ per year. The second, between December 2025 and February 2026, follows the release of models capable of extended autonomous work and is absent from the AI categories themselves. Since December 2025 submissions without a CS listing have run $17\%$ above trend, and in September 2026 total submissions reached a record $40\,363$. The excess is largest in mathematics, where submissions doubled within a year, and follows a gradient from formal and theoretical fields to experimental ones that is not ordered by surveyed rates of AI-tool adoption. In mathematics the increase is distributed across subfields and authors, two-thirds of it arising from a larger number of distinct authors rather than from a few prolific submitters. Across fields the clearest signature is a shift to single authorship: solo-authored papers rose by $70\%$ within a year in mathematics and condensed matter, and by $44\%$ in quantitative biology even as its total output fell, but not in experimental particle physics. The analysis is deliberately agnostic of LLM-detection methods: it uses only submission counts and metadata, with treatment timing fixed by calendar dates, and is therefore free of the outcome-triggered timing bias of author-level studies.

entry.title: Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data: preregistered measurements on EU law, Internet standards and retracted science
entry.summary: Official texts are corrected after publication: EU corrigenda, verified RFC errata, retractions. We measured whether these corrections are present in four public datasets used to train language models, and what models answer about the corrected passages. In EurlexResources, a legal training dataset, 1,989 of 2,082 testable single-language corrections to EU acts (95.5%, 94.6-96.3) remain in their erroneous form; in a random sample of 100, 46 change the meaning, a figure, a cross-reference, the competent authority or the scope (20 without scope). At least 124 corrected EU-law errors and at least 60 verified RFC errata (38 classified "Technical") are reproduced in their erroneous form in FineWeb-2 and in a sample of FineWeb. About 12,200 retracted papers (11,700-12,500) are present in the peS2o corpus, 79% with no mention of the retraction; separately, 53% of a random sample of retracted papers are still cited at least a year after retraction (OpenAlex). Asked 59 questions on serious corrected errors without documents, five models gave the erroneous version in 45% of the answers in which they committed to one version (31-60% allowing for clustering by question): 53% for scope corrections, 32% for the others. One answer in 295 said it did not know. Shown both versions side by side, the models chose the corrected one in 53% of cases (49-57), and naming the act made no difference; when each version carried its date and the corrigendum label, the four larger models chose it in 99-100% of cases. A comparison between a legal masked language model and its base model is null, against our bet: we do not show that model answers come from the datasets measured. All steps were preregistered and their fingerprints timestamped in the Bitcoin blockchain; six controls failed, several bets were lost, and every deviation is reported. Data and proofs: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23642239.

entry.title: From Data Footprints to Researcher Fingerprints: Temporal Ego-centric Research Group Detection in Scientific Knowledge Graphs
entry.summary: Understanding who researchers collaborate with, when and how their research groups form, and how these evolve over time is a foundational prerequisite for constructing multidimensional, evidence-based researcher fingerprints -- a requirement that has become increasingly urgent in the context of ongoing reforms in research evaluation advocated by initiatives such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA. In this paper, we propose an egocentric approach for fine-grained research group detection, operating at the scale of individual researchers' ego networks, as extracted from Scientific Knowledge Graphs (SKGs), and requiring the ego node to be present in all identified research groups -- a constraint that is not merely technical but reflects a commitment to researcher-centred analysis. Our approach builds on the Leiden algorithm as its computational core and is grounded in SKGs, which provide the heterogeneous, open scholarly metadata necessary to trace collaboration patterns at scale in a reproducible and transparent manner. We evaluate the proposed method through a user evaluation involving 10 researchers with diverse backgrounds and career stages, demonstrating its ability to surface meaningful and interpretable collaboration structures. The research groups identified constitute the structural scaffold upon which richer characterisations of scholarly identity -- including roles, seniority, contribution types, and publication patterns -- can be built in subsequent work, contributing to the broader goal of fairer and more transparent research assessment.
